demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Moana Tui is a 46-year-old married forensic analyst who came to treatment more than a year after her younger brother died suddenly in a violent accident. She had been the family member asked to identify him. What stayed with her was not a full narrative of that day but a set of brutal fragments: the fluorescent hum in the viewing room, the sound of her own breath turning ragged, and the clipped voice of a staff member saying her brother's name. In her mind, the memory returned as still pictures rather than a continuous sequence-the edge of the sheet, his hand, the unnatural color of his face. When it came back, she did not just see it; she sometimes heard the sounds from that room again, as if they had been preserved intact. The force of it was so immediate that she had to shut it down, turning away mid-thought or leaving the room because she felt flooded too quickly to bear it.

In the months after his death, Moana had come to believe that something fundamental had ended. She said her life had been destroyed by what happened, not in a dramatic sense but as a settled fact: the future she recognized was gone. She no longer felt any sustaining trust in people, in life, or in anything larger that might make suffering tolerable. Alongside that was a deadened conviction that nothing in her life meant much anymore. Those conclusions shaped how the memory sat inside her. Because she experienced the death as proof that life was empty and unsafe, the fragments of the viewing room came back with the force of that meaning attached to them, each snapshot feeling less like a past event than confirmation that everything had been permanently ruined. Even brief contact with the memory became overwhelming.

Her work made it hard to keep distance from anything associated with death. As a forensic analyst, she spent her days in labs and offices where case files, evidence logs, and matter-of-fact discussions about bodies were ordinary. She began avoiding work whenever she could, taking sick days, arriving late, and sometimes sitting in her car in the parking lot unable to make herself go in. The sterile lighting and clipped procedural language at work were close enough to the atmosphere of the identification room that she dreaded being pulled back into those frozen images and sounds. At home she started staying up very late, scrolling aimlessly or watching television until the early morning because sleep felt like surrendering control; in the quiet of bed, the pictures and the remembered voices came fastest. She also began restricting her eating, describing it less as hunger loss than as a way to keep herself tightly managed, numb, and contained.

These habits gradually tightened around her. By avoiding work and delaying sleep, Moana gave herself fewer chances to feel steady or competent, and the long nights left her more frayed, more vulnerable to the memory intruding without warning. Skipping meals added to the sense that she was running on fumes. When the snapshots returned, they seemed sharper, and the sounds in her head more vivid, at exactly the times she was most depleted. She would try to think about her brother and immediately hit that same wall of emotion, as though the memory could only arrive at full intensity. The more she organized her days around not going in, not sleeping, not eating, the less her life resembled the one she had before his death, and this seemed to prove to her that the trauma had in fact destroyed everything worth recognizing.

That conclusion fed the habits further. Because nothing felt meaningful anymore, work seemed pointless; because she had lost faith in life itself, caring for her body felt irrelevant; because she was certain her old life was gone, there seemed to be little reason to keep ordinary routines. Her husband had started pleading with her to eat dinner with him or come to bed before dawn, and she often withdrew from those conversations with a flat certainty that he could not understand what had been broken. Missing work had begun to draw attention from supervisors, which only deepened her sense that the life she had built was collapsing.

By the time she sought help, Moana was frightened by how small and barren her world had become. She was not coming with much hope in recovery; hope itself felt like something she had lost. But she was afraid that if nothing changed, she would lose her job, damage her marriage, and remain trapped with those few unbearable pictures and sounds of her brother's death as the only parts of him her mind would allow her to keep.
